content: Specific allergen immunotherapy (SIT) is a treatment approach that aims to improve the severity of atopic eczema (AE) by inducing immune tolerance to specific allergens. However, a high-quality systematic review evaluating the efficacy and safety of SIT for AE has not been conducted previously. The objective of this review was to assess the effects of SIT, administered via subcutaneous, sublingual, intradermal, or oral routes, compared to placebo or standard treatments in individuals with AE. The review included randomized controlled trials (RCTs) that used standardized allergen extracts in participants with AE. The databases searched included the Cochrane Skin Group Specialised Register, CENTRAL, MEDLINE, EMBASE, LILACS, Web of Science™, the GREAT database, and five trial registries, with searches conducted up to July 2015. Abstracts from recent allergy meetings and references from included studies were also reviewed. A total of 12 RCTs involving 733 participants were included in the review. The allergens targeted included house dust mite (10 trials), grass pollen, and other inhalant allergens (2 trials). SIT was administered subcutaneously in six trials, sublingually in four trials, orally in one trial, and intradermally in one trial. The overall risk of bias was moderate, with high rates of participant dropout and lack of blinding being the primary methodological concerns. The primary outcomes assessed were: (1) participantor parent-reported global assessment of disease severity at the end of treatment, (2) participantor parent-reported specific symptoms of eczema using subjective measures, and (3) adverse events, such as acute asthma episodes or anaphylaxis. SCORing Atopic Dermatitis (SCORAD) was used to measure the effects of AE, including area affected (A), intensity (B), and subjective symptoms like itch and sleeplessness (C). For participantor parent-reported global assessment of disease severity, one trial with 20 participants reported improvement in 78% (7/9) of those treated with SIT compared to 27% (3/11) in the placebo group (risk ratio [RR] 2.85, 95% confidence interval [CI] 1.02 to 7.96; P = 0.04). Another trial with 24 participants found no significant difference, with 62% (8/13) improvement in the SIT group versus 81% (9/11) in the placebo group (RR 0.75, 95% CI 0.45 to 1.26; P = 0.38). Due to high heterogeneity between these studies, a meta-analysis was not performed. The quality of evidence for this outcome was low. For participantor parent-reported specific symptoms of eczema, two trials with 184 participants found no significant improvement in SCORAD part C (mean difference [MD] -0.74, 95% CI -1.98 to 0.50) or sleep disturbance (MD -0.49, 95% CI -1.03 to 0.06) with SIT compared to placebo. Similarly, no improvement in itch severity (SCORAD part C) was observed (MD -0.24, 95% CI -1.00 to 0.52). However, one non-blinded study with 60 participants reported a reduction in itch (MD -4.20, 95% CI -3.69 to -4.71) and overall symptoms (P < 0.01) with SIT compared to no treatment. Due to high heterogeneity, these studies could not be pooled. The quality of evidence for this outcome was very low. Adverse events were reported in seven trials. Systemic reactions occurred in 6.4% (18/282) of participants treated with SIT compared to 7.1% (15/210) in the no-treatment group (RR 0.78, 95% CI 0.41 to 1.49). Local reactions were reported in 32.1% (90/280) of participants treated with SIT compared to 21.6% (44/204) in the no-treatment group (RR 1.27, 95% CI 0.89 to 1.81). The quality of evidence for both systemic and local adverse reactions was moderate. For the secondary outcome of investigatoror physician-rated global assessment of disease severity, six trials with 262 participants showed significant improvement with SIT (RR 1.48, 95% CI 1.16 to 1.88). However, no studies reported participantor parent-rated eczema severity using a published scale. Two studies (n = 184) used SCORAD part C, which was included as a primary outcome. Overall, the findings were inconclusive due to the small number of studies, variability in results, and methodological limitations. Subgroup analyses did not identify a specific allergen, age group, or disease severity level where SIT was more effective. Additionally, it was unclear whether sublingual immunotherapy was associated with more local adverse reactions compared to subcutaneous immunotherapy. In conclusion, the quality of evidence supporting SIT for AE was low, primarily due to inconsistent results, lack of blinding, and limited participant-centered outcome measures. While SIT may have some potential as a treatment for AE, the evidence is insufficient to draw definitive conclusions. Future studies should use high-quality allergen formulations with proven efficacy in other allergic conditions and include participant-reported outcome measures.
